headline: Scientists invent ultrasonic espresso at room temperature, no hot water needed.
summary: Researchers at UNSW developed 'ultrasonic espresso,' brewing coffee at room temperature using high-frequency sound waves. This method consumes 75% less energy than conventional techniques.
details: Colombian researcher Francisco Trujillo led a team at Australia’s University of New South Wales to invent "ultrasonic espresso." This room-temperature brewing process uses high-frequency sound waves to extract flavor, oils, aroma, and caffeine from ground coffee.

While taking longer (three minutes compared to 30 seconds for conventional espresso), the ultrasonic method consumes 75 percent less energy. This offers significant benefits for coffee shops, restaurants, and industrial producers of ready-to-drink coffee products.

The experimental system directs ultrasonic waves into a filter containing ground beans in water. It harnesses acoustic cavitation, where tiny bubbles form and collapse, generating microcurrents that facilitate the extraction of soluble compounds from the coffee.

Scientists designed a device to transmit ultrasonic vibrations throughout the entire filter basket, transforming it into an "acoustic reactor." This design allows waves to hit multiple points simultaneously, accelerating liquid movement around coffee particles and replacing heat with mechanical energy.

The goal was to achieve espresso-comparable concentration. Researchers adjusted variables like grind size, ultrasound power, and brewing time. Using a fine grind and 100 watts of power, they matched the dissolved solids and extraction yields ideal for specialty coffee.

Chemical analysis showed similar concentrations of caffeine and chlorogenic acid to conventional methods. No significant differences were observed in pH or the overall composition of volatile compounds responsible for the aroma.

Sensory tests with 100 participants compared ultrasonic and conventional espresso, revealing no notable preference for either method. However, for filtered coffee, the ultrasonically processed version was generally preferred, with participants rating its bitterness as more pleasant.

Beyond sensory replication, the new technique offers environmental advantages. Measurements indicate the ultrasonic system uses just 24 percent of the energy consumed by a typical espresso machine to produce beverages of the same intensity.

The research, detailed in the Journal of Food Engineering, suggests the possibility of new coffee makers. These could prepare espresso, filtered coffee, and cold brew using the same ultrasound technology, potentially replacing the characteristic sound of an espresso machine with inaudible vibrations.

headline_marked: [[AI model costs fell 280x]] in two years, but company AI bills are still rising
headline: AI model costs fell 280x in two years, but company AI bills are still rising
summary: Despite a 280-fold drop in AI model token prices over two years, average enterprise AI spending has increased by over 300%. This paradox is driven by increased usage from complex AI agents.
details: The cost of running a capable AI model has plummeted by roughly 280 times in two years, according to Stanford's 2026 AI Index. However, over the same period, the average company's AI bill has paradoxically gone up, not down. This economic shift is crucial for understanding AI spend in 2026.

The collapse in token prices is staggering, with GPT-3.5-level performance falling from $20 per million tokens to about 7 cents between Nov 2022 and Oct 2024. Epoch AI reports a median decline near 50 times per year, while a16z notes a 10x annual drop, faster than compute or bandwidth in previous eras.

Frontier models also saw significant price cuts; Anthropic's Claude Opus 4.5 reduced flagship prices by 67% in late 2025. This was largely driven by competition, with models like DeepSeek R1 offering high performance at significantly lower costs, forcing major labs to respond with emergency price adjustments.

By mid-2026, the cost floor is remarkably low: OpenAI's GPT-5.4-nano runs at 20 cents input per million, and DeepSeek V4 Pro (open-weights) is near 44 cents input. Google's Gemini 3.5 Flash also beats previous generations on agent benchmarks at competitive rates, making intelligence cheaper to rent than ever.

The paradox stems from how cheaper tokens are utilized: they are spent, not saved. The nature of AI interactions has evolved from single prompts to complex agentic workflows, involving 10-20 model calls for a single user task. These agents plan, use tools, check work, and often employ retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) to inflate context.

Furthermore, monitoring agents and always-on assistants bill around the clock, whether actively watched or not. This means that while the unit cost (per-token price) became hundreds of times cheaper, the number of units per job increased by even more, leading to higher overall expenditure.

This pattern mirrors historical efficiency gains in computing: cheaper storage led to ubiquitous video, and cheaper bandwidth enabled streaming. Similarly, cheaper intelligence isn't lowering AI spend; it's making sophisticated, 'hungry' agents economically viable, transforming a one-cent workload into a fifteen-cent loop that enhances product quality.
